Clinical Reference · Gastroenterology

Lower GI Bleed

On this page
Bleeding from a source distal to the ligament of Treitz — in modern usage, the colon, rectum, and anus (small-bowel sources are reclassified as "mid-GI") — presenting as hematochezia. Most is diverticular, most stops on its own (~75–80%), and the through-line of management is resuscitate first, localize second, and resist the urge to over-treat (no urgent scope, no TXA).
Diverticulosis = #1 cause (~30%) ~75–80% stop spontaneously Transfuse at Hb <7 g/dL (8 if CVD) Colonoscopy — non-urgent, after prep CTA → embolization if unstable Anchor: resuscitate · risk-stratify (Oakland) · localize
Shared

Pathophysiology

🧬

One symptom, several plumbing failures

"Lower GI bleed" is a presentation, not a diagnosis. The classic definition is bleeding from a source distal to the ligament of Treitz; modern practice splits that territory into mid-GI bleeding (ligament of Treitz → ileocecal valve = small bowel, the realm of capsule endoscopy) and true LGIB (ileocecal valve → anus = colon, rectum, anus). Blood that has not spent hours marinating in acid arrives fresh: bright-red or maroon hematochezia. The reassuring headline is that the colon is a low-pressure, forgiving organ — roughly 75–80% of colonic bleeds stop on their own, which is exactly why the guideline reflex is to resuscitate and localize rather than to rush a scope or reach for a hemostatic drug.

Where the diagnosis actually forks is the type of vessel that failed, and that fork dictates everything downstream:

  • Diverticular (~30%, the single most common) — an arterial bleed. Diverticula are mucosal herniations that punch through the colonic wall exactly where the vasa recta penetrate. The little artery is stretched, thin-walled, over the dome of the sac; when it ruptures the bleed is brisk, painless, and often self-limited once the vessel clots and retracts.
  • Angiodysplasia / vascular ectasia (~2–10%, more in the elderly, CKD, aortic stenosis, LVAD) — a venous/capillary problem. Chronic low-grade obstruction of submucosal veins produces dilated, tortuous, thin ectatic vessels. Bleeds are typically slower, recurrent, right-sided, and iron-deficiency-driven. High-shear states (aortic stenosis, LVAD) cleave von Willebrand multimers → acquired von Willebrand disease → these fragile vessels bleed even more (Heyde syndrome).
  • Ischemic colitis (~6–16%) — a perfusion failure, not a burst vessel. Low flow at the colonic watershed zones (splenic flexure = Griffiths point; rectosigmoid junction = Sudeck point) causes mucosal infarction that sloughs and oozes. The give-away is crampy pain then bloody diarrhea in an older vasculopath after a hypotensive insult.
  • Everything else — neoplasia/post-polypectomy (a cut artery in the polyp stalk), IBD and infectious colitis (inflamed friable mucosa), anorectal disease (hemorrhoids, fissures), and radiation proctitis (obliterative endarteritis → neovascular telangiectasias).
Think of the colon as old household plumbing. A diverticular bleed is a pinhole burst in a pressurized supply line — dramatic, but the pipe often self-seals. Angiodysplasia is a corroded, bulging drain vein that weeps — never a flood, but it keeps coming back and slowly empties the tank (anemia). Ischemic colitis is what happens when the water pressure to the whole house drops — the pipe furthest from the pump (the watershed) starves and the wall rots. You fix each with a different tool: patch the burst (clip), cauterize the weepy vein (argon plasma), or restore pressure to the house (fluids/blood, treat the shock).
The three dominant mechanisms of colonic bleeding and the therapy each one calls for. Note that only the arterial (diverticular) and ectatic (angiodysplasia) lesions get a device; ischemia is treated by fixing perfusion.
Colonic anatomy. The watershed zones (splenic flexure, rectosigmoid) are the boundaries between arterial territories — where ischemic colitis strikes. Right-colon lesions can present as melena or maroon stool because of transit time.
Original: BruceBlaus. When using this image in external sources it can be cited as: Bla..., Blausen 0603 LargeIntestine Anatomy-ar.png (CC BY 3.0), via Wikimedia Commons
Colonic diverticulum seen at colonoscopy — a mucosal outpouching at the point where the vasa recta penetrate the wall. A visible vessel or adherent clot in the dome is the endoscopic stigma of a diverticular bleed.
melvil, Colon diverticulum.jpg (CC BY-SA 4.0), via Wikimedia Commons
Argon plasma coagulation (APC) of a colonic vascular lesion — the workhorse treatment for angiodysplasia, which is too flat and diffuse to clip. Non-contact thermal coagulation seals the ectatic vessels.
Samir at English Wikipedia, Argon plasma coagulation.jpg (CC BY-SA 3.0), via Wikimedia Commons
Histology of acute severe ischemic colitis — mucosal necrosis and hemorrhage. Ischemia hits the superficial mucosa first (it is furthest from the submucosal blood supply), producing the segmental, watershed-distribution injury seen endoscopically.
CoRus13, Acute severe ischemic colitis, high mag.1.jpg (CC BY-SA 4.0), via Wikimedia Commons
The through-line for every therapy in this guide: because most colonic bleeds are self-limited and pressure-forgiving, the "drugs" that matter in LGIB are mostly not hemostatic agents — they are resuscitation and reversal. (1) Blood products replace what's lost and restore the very perfusion that lets the colon heal — but restrictively, because over-transfusion raises venous pressure and worsens rebleeding (Villanueva). (2) Anticoagulant reversal (4F-PCC, idarucizumab, andexanet) removes the one thing preventing the clot from forming. (3) Iron rebuilds the tank after chronic angiodysplastic loss. (4) Octreotide / thalidomide shrink the abnormal ectatic vessels themselves. The definitive "hemostasis" is mechanical — an endoscopic clip/band/APC or angiographic embolization of the feeding artery. Notably, tranexamic acid is NOT used (HALT-IT: no benefit, more clots and seizures) and PPIs have essentially no role in a lower source.

Etiology & approximate frequency

CauseApprox. frequencyVessel / mechanismClassic clue

Frequency ranges pooled across populations (ACG 2023; StatPearls; PMC6946606). Always remember a brisk upper source can masquerade as LGIB: ~10–15% of "hematochezia" is a fast UGIB — a normal BUN:Cr <20–30 and negative gastric aspirate argue against it.

Presentation — symptom / sign frequency & why it happens

Symptom / sign~FrequencyWhy it happens (pathophysiology)
Hematochezia (bright red / maroon per rectum)~90%+Fresh blood in the colon has no time to be oxidized/digested; bright red = distal/left, maroon = right colon or brisker transit
Painless bleeding~50–60%Diverticular and angiodysplastic bleeds are purely vascular — no inflammation, no peritoneal signal, so no pain
Crampy abdominal pain~20–40%Points to ischemic colitis or IBD/infectious colitis — the wall itself is injured/inflamed and distended
Hemodynamic changes (tachycardia, hypotension, orthostasis)~15–20%Acute intravascular volume loss; a marker of brisk/large-volume bleed and the trigger for resuscitation and CTA
Fatigue / dyspnea / pallor (anemia)~15–35%Chronic or subacute blood loss (classic for angiodysplasia); reduced oxygen-carrying capacity
Melena (with a lower source)<15%Slow right-colon bleeding dwells long enough for bacterial degradation of hemoglobin to hematin — a lower source can look "upper"
Syncope / presyncope~10%Rapid volume loss → transient cerebral hypoperfusion; a red flag for severe bleeding (a Strate predictor)
Diarrhea / urgency / tenesmus<15%Mucosal inflammation (colitis, radiation proctitis) drives secretion, motility, and rectal irritation

🩺 Clinic — outpatient hematochezia, recurrent bleeding & prevention
Assess

When to suspect & who

🔍

Outpatient presentation & risk

In clinic you meet the stable end of the spectrum: intermittent bright-red blood on the tissue or coating the stool, a positive screening FIT, or unexplained iron-deficiency anemia. Your two jobs are (1) decide whether this is a benign anorectal source safe to watch versus something that needs a structural evaluation, and (2) never miss a colorectal cancer or a bleed that is actually unstable and belongs in the ED.

PatternSuggestsAction
Bright red on paper, stops quickly, painful defecationHemorrhoids / fissureAnoscopy; conservative care — but still scope if ≥45 or anemia
Recurrent, painless, iron-deficiency anemia, elderlyAngiodysplasia / right-colon lesionColonoscopy; iron repletion; look for AS/CKD/LVAD
Change in bowel habits, weight loss, anemia, ≥45 yColorectal neoplasiaColonoscopy — do not defer to FIT
Crampy pain then bloody diarrhea, vasculopathIschemic colitisUsually presents acutely → ED / admit
Internal hemorrhoids (retroflexed endoscopic view) — the most common benign anorectal source of bright-red outlet bleeding. Diagnosis of exclusion in anyone screening-eligible.
Jmarchn, Internal hemorrhoids 2Grad, endoscopy.jpg (CC BY-SA 3.0), via Wikimedia Commons
Colorectal carcinoma narrowing the lumen. Occult or intermittent bleeding from a right-sided tumor classically presents as iron-deficiency anemia — the reason overt or occult LGIB in a screening-age adult mandates colonoscopy.

Visible rectal bleeding is never adequately worked up by a FIT. FIT is a screening test for asymptomatic average-risk adults; in someone who is actually bleeding, a negative FIT is falsely reassuring — they still need a colonoscopy.

Treat

Chronic / recurrent bleeding

💊

Recurrent angiodysplasia — first-line → escalation

The outpatient "chronic management" of LGIB is really the management of recurrent, transfusion-dependent angiodysplastic bleeding (and iron repletion for anyone with iron-deficiency from GI loss). Diverticular bleeds don't get chronic drug therapy — they either recur and get scoped/embolized, or they don't.

1
First-line — iron repletion + endoscopic ablation
Fill the tank; cauterize what you can see.
▾
Iron doesn't stop the bleeding — it restores the hemoglobin the slow ectatic vessels keep draining, keeping the patient out of the transfusion cycle. Argon plasma coagulation seals accessible lesions non-contact.
DrugStartTitrate / targetWhy it worksIf intolerant / alt
Ferrous sulfate325 mg (65 mg elemental) PO daily or every other dayContinue until ferritin >100 & anemia resolved, then ~3 mo to refill storesReplaces iron lost to chronic bleeding; alternate-day dosing improves absorption (lower hepcidin)Ferrous gluconate 324 mg (38 mg elem.) or ferrous fumarate 324 mg (106 mg elem.) if GI upset
IV iron (ferric carboxymaltose)750 mg IV ×2 (≥7 d apart) or 1000 mg (iron sucrose 200 mg ×5)Repeat per iron deficit / Ganzoni; recheck ferritin in 4–8 wkBypasses gut when losses outpace oral absorption or oral is not tolerated — the usual reality in ongoing angiodysplasiaIron sucrose or ferric derisomaltose; premedicate only if prior reaction
Argon plasma coagulationEndoscopic, at index colonoscopyRepeat for recurrence (multifocal disease is common)Non-contact thermal coagulation of flat ectatic vessels too diffuse to clipBipolar/heater probe; band ligation for discrete lesions
2
If recurrent despite ablation — octreotide
Shrink splanchnic inflow to the lesions.
▾
Somatostatin analogues reduce splanchnic blood flow and improve platelet aggregation/angiogenesis signaling — the OCEAN RCT (2023) showed long-acting octreotide cut transfusion requirements in recurrent angiodysplastic bleeding.
DrugStartTargetWhy it worksAlt
Octreotide LAR20 mg IM q4 wk (or short-acting 50–100 mcg SC BID bridge)40 mg IM q28 d if inadequate; assess transfusion need over 6 mo↓Splanchnic flow to ectatic vessels; pro-hemostaticLanreotide
3
Refractory / transfusion-dependent — thalidomide, treat the driver
Anti-angiogenic; fix Heyde.
▾
Thalidomide is anti-angiogenic (anti-VEGF): the 2023 NEJM RCT showed ~71% achieved >50% reduction in bleeding vs 4% with iron alone — but adverse effects (constipation, neuropathy, somnolence, VTE) limit it to true refractory cases. Fix the mechanical driver where present: aortic valve replacement reverses Heyde syndrome; optimize CKD; address LVAD-associated acquired vWD.
OptionDoseWhy / evidenceCaution
Thalidomide50–100 mg PO daily × ~4 moAnti-VEGF; NEJM 2023 RCT positiveVTE, neuropathy, teratogen (REMS)
Aortic valve replacementProceduralRestores vWF multimers → reverses HeydePerioperative risk assessment
BevacizumabCase-basedAnti-VEGF for refractory diseaseLimited evidence
Anticoagulation resumption after a bleed. Restart is generally recommended once hemostasis is secure — not resuming increases thromboembolism and mortality, and observational data show restarting (especially DOACs) does not meaningfully raise rebleeding. The usual window is ~7–14 days, individualized on thrombotic risk (mechanical valve, recent VTE, CHA₂DS₂-VASc) versus whether the source was definitively treated. Continue aspirin taken for secondary cardiovascular prevention.
Monitor

Follow-up & recheck cadence

📈

What to recheck, and when

  • CBC — 2–4 weeks after starting iron (expect Hb ↑ ~1 g/dL every 2–3 wk); ferritin at ~8–12 weeks to confirm store repletion.
  • Symptom diary — episodes/severity of bleeding to gauge octreotide/thalidomide response and transfusion frequency over months.
  • Surveillance colonoscopy — per polyp/cancer pathology if a neoplasm or polyps were found; otherwise no routine re-scope for a single treated diverticular bleed.
  • Screen the drivers — echocardiogram for aortic stenosis (Heyde) in recurrent angiodysplasia; iron studies each cycle.
Prevent

USPSTF A/B & prevention

🛡️

Colorectal cancer screening (USPSTF 2021)

GradeRecommendationPopulation
AScreen for colorectal cancerAll adults 50–75 y
BScreen for colorectal cancer (new in 2021)Adults 45–49 y
CSelectively offer screening (individualize)Adults 76–85 y

Modalities & intervals: colonoscopy q10y · FIT annually · high-sensitivity gFOBT annually · stool DNA-FIT (Cologuard) q1–3y · CT colonography q5y · flexible sigmoidoscopy q5y (or q10y + annual FIT). Any abnormal non-colonoscopy test → follow-up colonoscopy.

Screening prevents the most common serious cause of outpatient LGIB — colorectal cancer — and turns a future emergency into a resected polyp. It is the single highest-value prevention lever in this disease.
Escalate

When to send to the ED / admit

🚑

Red flags & the Oakland safe-discharge score

Do not manage in clinic — send to ED — with any of: hemodynamic instability (HR >100, SBP <100, orthostasis), large-volume or ongoing brisk bleeding, syncope, symptomatic anemia (chest pain, dyspnea, dizziness), anticoagulation with active bleeding, or age >50 with new significant bleeding.

Oakland Score — safe discharge in acute LGIB

Oakland K et al., Lancet Gastroenterol Hepatol 2017 / BSG 2019. Range 0–35. A score ≤8 predicts ~95% probability of safe discharge for outpatient workup.

🛏️ Wards — acute inpatient resuscitation, localization & hemostasis
Admit

Who to admit

📋

Admission criteria & initial profile

Admit any acute LGIB that is not a clearly benign, self-limited outlet bleed in a low-risk patient (Oakland ≤8). Concretely, admit for:

  • Hemodynamic changes: HR ≥100, SBP ≤115 (or a drop from baseline), orthostasis, or syncope.
  • Ongoing or large-volume hematochezia, or requiring transfusion.
  • Significant anemia (Hb drop, symptomatic) or a high-risk profile: anticoagulation/coagulopathy, ≥2 active comorbidities, age >60.
  • Oakland score >8 or Strate high-risk features (see calculator in Clinic).
Two numbers decide the level of care immediately: shock index (HR/SBP >1 = concerning) and the BUN:Cr ratio (>30 → strongly consider an upper source and get an NG lavage or upper endoscopy first — a nasogastric aspirate that is bilious and clear lowers the odds of an active upper bleed).

Treat

Acute management

💊

Resuscitate → correct → localize → treat

1
Resuscitate & transfuse — restrictively
The first and most evidence-based intervention.
▾
Restoring circulating volume restores the very perfusion the colon needs to heal, but over-transfusion raises portal/venous pressure and worsens rebleeding — Villanueva 2013 showed a restrictive threshold (Hb <7) cut mortality (5% vs 9%) and rebleeding (10% vs 16%) vs a liberal (Hb <9) strategy.
ProductTrigger / targetNotesWhyException
Packed RBCsTransfuse Hb <7; target 7–9 g/dL1 unit ≈ ↑Hb 1 g/dL; recheck after eachRestrictive = better survival & less rebleeding (Villanueva, TRICC)Hb <8 if cardiovascular disease / ACS or unstable
PlateletsKeep ≥30 ×10⁹/L (severe active bleed); ≥50 before endoscopic therapy≥100 if CNS bleed / massive transfusionEnables primary hemostasis / procedural safetyAdd DDAVP 0.3 mcg/kg if uremic platelet dysfunction
CrystalloidBalanced fluid to bridge to bloodAvoid over-resuscitation with salineMaintains perfusion until product available—
Do NOT give tranexamic acid. HALT-IT (2020, n=12,009): no reduction in death from bleeding (RR 0.99), with more venous thromboembolism (0.8% vs 0.4%) and seizures (RR 1.73). And skip the PPI — it has no role in a confirmed lower source.
2
Reverse coagulopathy — only if life-threatening
Remove the block to clotting; don't over-correct.
▾
Endoscopy is safe at INR ≤2.5 and you should not delay it to correct mild–moderate coagulopathy. Reserve full reversal for life-threatening bleeding or hemodynamic instability — reversal itself carries thrombotic risk.
Agent on boardReversalDoseWhy it worksAdjunct
Warfarin (VKA)4-factor PCC (preferred over FFP)25 / 35 / 50 units/kg for INR 2–4 / 4–6 / >6Replaces vitamin-K-dependent factors II, VII, IX, X instantly+ Vitamin K 10 mg IV (sustains correction)
DabigatranIdarucizumab5 g IV (2 × 2.5 g)Monoclonal Fab binds dabigatran directlyDialysis (dabigatran is dialyzable) if unavailable
Apixaban / rivaroxaban (factor Xa inhibitors)Andexanet alfaLow: 400 mg bolus + 4 mg/min ×2 h · High: 800 mg + 8 mg/minDecoy Xa sequesters the inhibitor4F-PCC 50 units/kg if andexanet unavailable
Heparin / LMWHProtamine sulfate1 mg per 100 U heparin (max 50 mg); partial for LMWHPositively charged; neutralizes heparin—
3
Localize & achieve hemostasis
Colonoscopy — non-urgent; CTA/IR if unstable.
▾
For the stable patient, colonoscopy after adequate prep is diagnostic and therapeutic — but it need not be urgent: Niikura 2020 and multiple RCTs/meta-analyses show colonoscopy <24 h does not reduce rebleeding or mortality (and trended toward more rebleeding), so do the next-available quality colonoscopy after prep. For the unstable or brisk bleeder who can't be prepped, go to CTA → angioembolization (see ICU).
  • Endoscopic hemostasis: through-the-scope or over-the-scope clips and band ligation for diverticular bleeding and post-polypectomy stalks; argon plasma coagulation for angiodysplasia and radiation proctitis; epinephrine 1:10,000 injection only as an adjunct (never monotherapy — it's temporary vasoconstriction); TC-325 hemostatic spray for diffuse or rescue oozing.
  • Defer colonoscopy if bleeding has stopped and a high-quality colonoscopy within 12 months already showed diverticulosis without neoplasia.
Monitor

Daily management

📈

What to trend each day

  • Hemoglobin trajectory — serial CBC (q4–12h while active, then daily). A stable Hb across two checks off transfusion is the key stability signal.
  • Hemodynamics & stool output — HR, BP, orthostatics; number and character of bloody stools (fresh red vs darkening = slowing).
  • Transfusion tally — units/24h; ongoing requirement is an ICU/IR trigger.
  • Coags & platelets — after reversal/products; ensure INR ≤2.5 before any planned scope.
  • Resume home meds — plan anticoagulation restart timing (see Clinic) once hemostasis secure.
Escalate

When to call ICU

⬆️

Escalation triggers

Transfer to ICU/step-down for any of:
  • Persistent hemodynamic instability despite ≥2 L crystalloid / ongoing hypotension (SBP <90) or shock index >1.
  • Ongoing transfusion requirement — e.g., ≥2–4 units RBC in 24 h to maintain Hb, or any massive transfusion (≥4 units/hr or ≥10 units/24h).
  • Brisk, ongoing hematochezia requiring CTA/angioembolization or urgent intervention.
  • Need for vasopressor support, airway protection (massive bleeding/aspiration risk), or serious comorbidity destabilizing (ACS, decompensated cirrhosis).
Dispo

Discharge & disposition

🏠

Readiness + where they go

Discharge readiness: no hematochezia for ~24 h, hemodynamically stable, Hb stable across ≥2 checks without transfusion, coagulopathy addressed, source identified/treated (or low-risk with an outpatient colonoscopy plan), tolerating diet, and a clear anticoagulation-resumption plan.

Home

Stable, bleeding stopped, reliable follow-up; outpatient colonoscopy arranged if not done.

Home health

Home + nursing for IV iron infusions, anticoagulation monitoring, or frailty support.

SNF

Deconditioned elderly needing 24h skilled nursing after a prolonged bleed.

Acute rehab (IRF)

Rarely needed unless a complicating event (e.g., peri-arrest, stroke) added a rehab need.

LTAC

Prolonged complex course (post-surgical, ventilator weaning after massive bleed).

Hospice / palliative

Recurrent bleeding in advanced malignancy or end-stage disease where goals are comfort-focused.
🫀 ICU — massive hemorrhage, resuscitation & source control
Admit

ICU triggers

🚨

When it belongs in the unit

LGIB reaches the ICU when the bleed outpaces the colon's tendency to self-resolve. Triggers:

  • Hemorrhagic shock — persistent SBP <90 or shock index >1 despite initial resuscitation; lactate ↑, altered mentation, oliguria.
  • Ongoing transfusion requirement — ≥2–4 units RBC/24h to hold Hb, or activation of the massive transfusion protocol (≥4 units/hr or ≥10 units/24h).
  • Brisk, ongoing hematochezia needing emergent CTA/angioembolization or unable to be prepped/scoped safely.
  • Need for vasopressors, airway protection, or a destabilizing comorbidity (ACS, decompensated cirrhosis).
Monitor

Monitoring & access

🩸

Lines, labs, targets

  • Access: two large-bore peripheral IVs (≥16–18 g) remain the fastest route for volume; add a central line (introducer/Cordis for rapid transfuser) and an arterial line for beat-to-beat BP and frequent labs.
  • Trend: serial CBC q1–2h during active bleeding, lactate/clearance, ionized calcium (citrate chelation during massive transfusion), fibrinogen, INR/PTT, ABG, urine output.
  • Targets: MAP ≥65, Hb ≥7 (≥8 if cardiac disease), platelets ≥50 (≥100 if massive/CNS), fibrinogen >150 mg/dL, ionized Ca²⁺ >1.1 mmol/L, normothermia, pH >7.2 — reverse the "lethal triad" (acidosis, hypothermia, coagulopathy).
Support

Pressors — a bridge, not the fix

💉

Which drip, why, and the dose

In hemorrhagic shock the definitive treatment is blood and source control — pressors only buy time. Use the minimum pressor to keep MAP ≥65 while product and IR/endoscopy are mobilized; leaning on vasopressors instead of transfusing masks the deficit and worsens tissue ischemia.
AgentReceptors / mechanismDose rangeHemodynamic effectWhen to pick
Norepinephrineα1 ≫ β10.01–0.5 mcg/kg/min↑SVR, modest ↑CO/HRFirst-line temporizing pressor while transfusing
VasopressinV1 receptor (non-adrenergic)0.03 units/min (fixed)↑SVR; splanchnic vasoconstrictionAdd-on to spare catecholamine dose; reduces splanchnic inflow
Epinephrineα1, β1, β20.01–0.5 mcg/kg/min↑CO, ↑SVR, ↑HRRefractory shock / peri-arrest bridge
Norepinephrine's α1-mediated vasoconstriction restores perfusion pressure without the tachyarrhythmia burden of pure β-agonists; vasopressin acts through a separate V1 pathway, so it adds tone when catecholamine receptors are downregulated by acidosis. Neither replaces the lost red cells.
Resus

Massive transfusion & airway

🩸

Balanced resuscitation targets

When bleeding is massive, transfuse in a balanced 1:1:1 ratio (RBC : plasma : platelets) to avoid dilutional coagulopathy, and give calcium — citrated products chelate ionized calcium, and hypocalcemia impairs both clotting and cardiac contractility.

Ratio
1 : 1 : 1
RBC : FFP : platelets
Calcium
iCa >1.1
replace during MTP
Fibrinogen
>150 mg/dL
cryo if low
Temp / pH
>36°C / >7.2
break the lethal triad

Airway: LGIB rarely needs intubation, but consider it for airway protection in massive hemorrhage with altered mentation, before urgent endoscopy in an unstable patient, or for aspiration risk during upper-source evaluation. If intubated for the procedure, standard lung-protective settings apply (AC/VC, 6 mL/kg IBW, PEEP 5, FiO₂ titrated to SpO₂ 92–96%).

Rescue

Source control — CTA, embolization, surgery

⚙️

Localize then occlude the feeding vessel

1
CT angiography — the first test in the unstable brisk bleeder
Localizes without prep.
▾
CTA needs active bleeding of roughly 0.3–0.5 mL/min to show contrast extravasation; sensitivity ~90% for hemodynamically significant bleeding. It requires no bowel prep, is fast, and — critically — maps the culprit vessel to guide the interventional radiologist. Yield is low in minor/intermittent bleeding, so reserve it for the brisk bleeder.
Catheter mesenteric angiography. A positive CTA should be followed promptly by transcatheter arteriography — angiography is ~9× more likely to localize the source if done within ~90 minutes of a positive CTA.
Omar Oda, Stenosis of the superior mesenteric artery.jpg (CC BY 2.0), via Wikimedia Commons

Tagged RBC (Tc-99m) scintigraphy is more sensitive for slow bleeding (~0.1–0.2 mL/min) but localizes poorly and is slow — largely supplanted by CTA in the ACG 2023 pathway.

2
Transcatheter arterial embolization (TAE)
Definitive without surgery.
▾
Superselective embolization of the bleeding vessel achieves ~98–100% technical success. Use microcoils (lowest ischemia rate, ~3%) rather than Gelfoam (higher ischemia); the main risk is bowel ischemia (~5% superselective). It is the fastest definitive option in the unstable patient and avoids an operation.
3
Endoscopic rescue & surgery — last resort
When localized / when nothing else works.
▾
  • Endoscopic hemostasis (if stable enough / after prep): clips, band ligation, argon plasma coagulation, TC-325 spray, epinephrine injection as adjunct only.
  • Surgery — reserved for uncontrolled bleeding failing endoscopic + angiographic control, or recurrent severe bleeding from an identified segment. Segmental colectomy if the source is localized; subtotal/total colectomy if unlocalized (higher morbidity; historical mortality ~20%). Always exhaust localization first — blind subtotal colectomy is a disaster if the source was actually upper.
Downgrade

When to downgrade

⬇️

De-escalation to the floor

Downgrade to the floor when: hemodynamically stable off vasopressors for ≥6–12 h, no active bleeding, Hb stable across ≥2 checks without transfusion, coagulopathy corrected/controlled, lactate cleared, and source controlled (embolized/scoped) or clearly self-limited.

Not yet if: still requiring transfusion to hold Hb, ongoing hematochezia, pressor-dependent, or awaiting a planned intervention (colonoscopy/angio) where re-bleeding would be catastrophic. ICU disposition for the rare refractory case: post-operative LTAC pathway or a goals-of-care conversation if recurrent bleeding in advanced/terminal disease.
Shared

Diagnostic pathway & comorbidities

🧭

Stable vs unstable — the whole algorithm on one page

The single fork that organizes LGIB management is hemodynamic stability. The stable patient is prepped and scoped on a normal timeline; the unstable brisk bleeder skips the prep and goes to CT angiography and interventional radiology.

LGIB algorithm (ACG 2023). Stability decides the branch: prep-and-scope for the stable patient; CTA-then-embolization for the unstable brisk bleeder.
🔗

Comorbidity interactions

Comorbidities change both the course and the management of LGIB — they alter transfusion targets, reversal strategy, and which drugs are dangerous.

ComorbidityHow it changes the bleedHow it changes management
Cardiovascular disease / ACSPoor tolerance of anemia; ischemia risk with hypotensionRaise transfusion threshold to Hb <8; continue secondary-prevention aspirin; balance DAPT interruption against stent thrombosis
Aortic stenosis (Heyde syndrome)High shear cleaves vWF → acquired vWD → angiodysplasia bleeds moreSuspect with recurrent right-colon bleeds; aortic valve replacement can cure it; consider vWF studies
Chronic kidney disease / ESRDUremic platelet dysfunction + higher angiodysplasia rateDDAVP 0.3 mcg/kg for uremic platelets; caution with renally-cleared anticoagulants; IV iron often needed
Cirrhosis / coagulopathyThrombocytopenia, prolonged INR (rebalanced hemostasis)INR poorly reflects bleeding risk; use platelets/fibrinogen and clinical judgment; avoid over-transfusion (portal pressure)
Atrial fibrillation / VTE on anticoagulationBleeds are larger and harder to stopReverse only if life-threatening; resume anticoagulation ~7–14 d after hemostasis (thrombosis risk > rebleed risk)
LVADContinuous-flow shear → acquired vWD + angiodysplasia; recurrent GI bleeding is commonReduce anticoagulation intensity carefully with cardiology; APC/octreotide for angiodysplasia; avoid stopping antithrombotics abruptly (pump thrombosis)
Drugs to avoid / use with caution in LGIB:
  • Tranexamic acid — not recommended (HALT-IT: no benefit, ↑VTE and seizures).
  • NSAIDs — stop; they cause and worsen colonic (and diverticular) bleeding and impair platelets.
  • Over-transfusion / liberal RBC targets — worse mortality and rebleeding (Villanueva); stay restrictive.
  • Routine full anticoagulant reversal for non-life-threatening bleeds — reversal carries thrombotic risk; endoscopy is safe at INR ≤2.5.
  • PPIs — no role once an upper source is excluded; don't reflexively continue them.
  • Bowel-cleansing avoidance — don't scope an unprepped colon in a stable patient (poor yield, missed lesions); prep first.

Landmark trials

TrialYearResultWhy it matters
Villanueva (NEJM)2013Restrictive (Hb <7) vs liberal (Hb <9) in acute GI bleed: 45-day mortality 5% vs 9% (HR 0.55), rebleeding 10% vs 16%Foundation for the restrictive transfusion threshold in GI bleeding; extrapolated to LGIB
TRIGGER (Lancet)2015Cluster-RCT: restrictive (Hb <8) vs liberal (Hb <10) feasible & safe; less RBC use, no worse outcomesConfirmed restrictive strategy feasible in real-world UGIB
TRICC (NEJM)1999Restrictive (Hb <7) vs liberal (Hb <10) in critically ill: equal/better survival, fewer cardiac events with restrictiveUnderpins restrictive ICU transfusion practice
HALT-IT (Lancet)2020TXA vs placebo in GI bleed (n=12,009): no reduction in death (RR 0.99); ↑VTE (0.8% vs 0.4%), ↑seizures (RR 1.73)Tranexamic acid should NOT be used for GI bleeding
Niikura (Gastroenterology)2020Early (<24h) vs elective colonoscopy: no difference in rebleeding/mortality (rebleed 15.3% vs 6.7%, NS — trend toward more with early)Urgent colonoscopy has no outcome benefit → non-emergent scope
Strate risk model2003–057 predictors of severe LGIB (HR≥100, SBP≤115, syncope, non-tender abdomen, bleeding <4h, aspirin, ≥2 comorbidities); 0 factors ~9% vs >3 ~84% riskEarly bedside risk stratification for severe bleeding
Thalidomide RCT (NEJM)2023Thalidomide vs iron for recurrent angiodysplasia: 71% vs 4% achieved >50% reduction in bleeding episodesAnti-angiogenic option for refractory transfusion-dependent angiodysplasia
